text: The lakefront that became Hyde Park stayed empty a while longer.
The sand that made the portage a crossing made this ground poor for crops.
An early settler named Nathan Watson tried to farm it, near the Chicago-to-Detroit wagon road, around what is now 53rd Street and Lake Park.
That road was not new.

It followed the old Sauk Trail, the Native footpath that ran from the Mississippi at Rock Island east to the Detroit River, the same kind of trail the Potawatomi had walked for generations before a surveyor ever touched it.
Watson dreamed of an orchard.
The sand beat him.
He turned his place into a tavern for travelers on the road.
When he died, his widow, Electa Watson, kept it as a boarding house and farm, the only real structure for miles along that stretch of shore.
Around it was the same country the Potawatomi had known.
Sand ridges with bur oaks, swales of wildflowers, prairie to the horizon.
That is the ground a young lawyer found in 1853.
Paul Cornell rode six miles south from the city most mornings to buy a glass of buttermilk from Electa Watson at the tavern.
In August of that year he bought three hundred acres of lakefront that no one else wanted, sinking nearly everything he had into it.

He named the place Hyde Park, after the London park, and within a few years he deeded sixty of those acres to the Illinois Central Railroad for a depot at 53rd Street and a commitment of daily trains to the city.
The grocery clerks and the elevated trains and the university were still decades off.
The bur oaks and the wildflowers were already there.
So was the deed, passed from a tavern keeper's widow to a man with a plan.
The first taking had set the pattern.
This ground would be claimed, cleared, and remade, by whoever held the paper, again and again.
